notes:
I couldn't finish this research, so these notes are incomplete. I ran out of searches and page reads. The pages I did open (Enduring Word, the Pulpit Commentary on Bible Hub and Precept Austin's Luke 23) were cut off before they reached verse 29. So for those three, the notes below rely only on the search previews. I found nothing usable for verses 29–31, 37–38, 47–49 or 54–56. I also found nothing from Methodist or Pentecostal teachers, from modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, NET notes), from Catholic or Orthodox sites, or about prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those verses and views are left out.

**v. 32–33**
- Guzik says Jesus was never a victim of circumstances on the cross: He was in control. Jesus said of His life in John 10:18, *no one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 34**
- Guzik: in this prayer Jesus recognized the blindness of His enemies. That didn't make them less guilty, but Jesus put them in the best possible light. Guzik says believers should pray the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- On the garments: even His clothes were taken. Guzik says Jesus let go of absolutely everything – even His clothes – becoming completely poor for us, so we could become completely rich in Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 35**
- Guzik on the rulers' taunt: it was precisely because He did *not* save Himself that He can save others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 36**
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks Luke's mention of sour wine means the soldiers were mocking Jesus' thirst. They held their wine up to His lips and then snatching them hastily away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/23.htm

**v. 39–41**
- Guzik notes that Matthew 27:44 and Mark 15:32 say both criminals mocked Jesus at first. Over the hours on the cross, one changed his mind and trusted Him. Guzik lists what this man showed: he feared God, admitted his own sin, saw that Jesus was innocent, and called out to Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- Precept Austin draws a lesson from the thieves: like them, we justly deserved the "death penalty" (Ro 6:23), yet because God's wrath fell on Christ, we receive eternal life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-23-commentary

**v. 42**
- The Pulpit Commentary says most older manuscripts leave out "Lord." It argues the sense is "remember me when you come *in* your kingdom," not "into." On this reading the thief was looking ahead to Christ's return in royal glory. He asks for no special place, he only asks the King not to forget him then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/23.htm
- Writing at 1517 (a Lutheran site), one author argues that the kingdom of God is not a place, a thing, a concept... The kingdom of God is a person. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-preaching-thief-on-the-cross

**v. 43: the traditional reading**
- Guzik calls this one deathbed conversion in the Bible, so that no one would despair; but *only one*, so that no one would presume. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- Spurgeon stresses that the man was a thief, saved at the point of death, yet received in no inferior way, and received into bliss in no secondary style. He takes "paradise" to mean heaven, pointing to Paul's use of the word in 2 Corinthians 12. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-43.html
- Ligonier says salvation comes *immediately* at death because Christ's work is sufficient. The thief had no chance to do good works. "Paradise" points to Eden, and the promise is of a restored, escalated Eden. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-does-luke-23-43-mean
- Barnes draws two lessons. The soul exists apart from the body, and the souls of the righteous are made happy straight after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-43.html
- Guzik (Q&A page) says the thief was not waiting for future resurrection. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/correcting-my-mistakes-qa-for-january-6-2022/
- A Bible Hub article separates the "intermediate state" from the final resurrection of the body. The thief's soul would be with Christ at once, while his body waited for the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/q/how_did_jesus_promise_instant_paradise.htm

**v. 43: where the comma goes (a disputed reading)**
- Some put the comma after "today," giving "I tell you today, you will be…". Gill rejects this. He says it is only contrived to serve an hypothesis, unlike Christ's usual way of speaking, and against all copies and versions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-43.html
- Clarke treats the verse as strong proof that the soul is not material. He says those who hold the opposite view try to explain this meaning away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-43.html
- Two translations do punctuate it the other way. Lamsa reads Truly I say to you today, you will be with me in Paradise. Rotherham has a similar wording. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/luke/23-43.html

**v. 43: a real Protestant difference over baptism**
- **Anglican (Ryle, hosted on a Reformed site):** This thief was never baptized. He belonged to no visible Church. He never received the Lord's Supper. Ryle's point is that he had faith, and so he was saved. Ryle also warns against presuming on a late conversion, since the other thief was lost. https://www.monergism.com/christ-and-two-thieves-luke-2339-43
- **Lutheran (1517):** this author expects the objection that the thief was never baptized. He answers with the Lutheran saying "It is not the lack of Baptism that damns, but the denial of it." He argues the thief was crucified with Christ and given the same promise as the baptized: You and the thief were baptized with the same Word. https://www.1517.org/articles/baptizing-the-thief-on-the-cross

**v. 44**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the darkness lasted from the sixth to the ninth hour, which is from 12 noon to 3 p.m. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/23.htm

**v. 44–45**
- The Pulpit Commentary quotes Godet: the darkness and the torn veil come from the deep link between Christ and humanity, and between humanity and nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/23.htm
- Guzik says the torn veil means two things. First, now man has free access to the throne of grace by the cross. Second, no one should ever think again that God dwells in temples made with hands. He also describes the Father laying on Jesus all the guilt and wrath that sin deserved. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 46**
- Guzik: Jesus gave up His life when He wanted to and how He wanted to. No one took His life from Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- Precept Austin quotes Guzik: because Jesus was sinless, death had no rightful claim on Him, so He could only die by giving up His spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-23-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary places these words just after "It is finished!" It calls them His entrance greeting to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/23.htm
- The Church Pulpit Commentary takes the verse as proof that the soul lives on after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/luke-23.html

**v. 50–53**
- Guzik quotes Geldenhuys praising quiet followers like Joseph, Nicodemus and the women, who served Jesus in love whatever it cost. Guzik's application is to serve Jesus in whatever way we actually can, as Joseph did, rather than waiting for some grand opportunity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

To fill the gaps, the next pages to read would be the full Enduring Word, Pulpit Commentary and Precept Austin pages (all linked above, from v. 29 on). After those, Bible Hub's Gill and Ellicott entries for verses 29–31 and 45, NET Bible notes, and New Advent or Catholic.com on the good thief.
